messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Pharmacist
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

Vignette:
Tane is a 24-year-old pharmacist who came to treatment months after the death of someone he loved, carrying a sense that his life had split into a before and an after that he could no longer join together. He is a single young man from an Oceanian family living in the United States, and when he speaks about the event he does so in fragments, as if the worst parts refuse to line up in order. He can say where he was, that there had been drinking, that other people were acting badly, and that someone he loved was harmed, but when he tries to make it into a clear story he loses the thread. At times he goes quiet and looks almost detached from what he is saying, describing it later as remembering it “like it happened to somebody else.” At other moments, the same memory floods him with guilt so sharply that he cannot stay with it for long. He has come to believe that he should have done something differently, noticed something earlier, prevented what happened somehow, even though when he tries to explain exactly how, his account breaks apart.

What remains vivid are not tidy facts but sharp impressions that seize him in the present. The smell of alcohol is especially potent. In the pharmacy where he works, he braces himself when customers approach the counter smelling of liquor, and even the scent of alcohol-based products can jolt him before he has had time to think. He describes his body as reacting first: his chest tightens, his muscles go rigid, and he feels suddenly prepared for danger even when he knows he is standing under fluorescent lights at work, filling routine prescriptions. He is embarrassed by how often this happens. A customer speaking too loudly, acting entitled, or ignoring basic rules can provoke the same surge. What disturbs him is not only the fear but the moral charge of it. Seeing people misbehave, especially in ways that feel selfish or reckless, stirs something immediate and physical in him. He is certain in those moments that people can do terrible damage without caring, and his body seems to respond as if that damage is about to happen again.

Funerals and cemeteries have become unbearable terrain. In the period after the death, he attended grief-related gatherings because he felt he should, but each one left him shaken. The sight of floral arrangements, rows of chairs, subdued clothing, and mourners greeting one another was enough to make him feel unreal and trapped at the same time. Eventually he began finding reasons not to go. When relatives or family friends mentioned memorial services, he told them his work schedule at the pharmacy was too demanding. He has avoided cemeteries altogether. This has narrowed his world in ways other people have noticed. Family members have read his absences as distance or indifference, and Tane has not been able to explain that what stops him is not lack of love but the fear of what happens inside him when grief is publicly marked.

Over time he has felt less and less like the person he was before. He says he used to be happy and easy with people, but now he moves through days with a constant sense of misery and strain. Even on ordinary shifts he feels keyed up, his body tense and ready, as though danger might emerge from nowhere. He knows that many of these moments are false alarms, but that knowledge arrives after the reaction, not before. He has started to think of his life as destroyed by what happened, not in the dramatic sense of everything collapsing at once, but in the slow, deadened sense that nothing feels meaningful anymore. The work he trained for feels mechanical. He counts tablets, counsels patients, answers questions, and goes home, all while feeling cut off from the reasons any of it should matter.

What finally brought him to seek help was not a single crisis but the accumulation of these moments until they seemed to define every week. Recently, during a shift, a customer who smelled strongly of alcohol became argumentative at the counter, and Tane felt his body surge into alarm so fast that he had to step away and let a coworker take over. Afterward he was shaken by how little it took and by how completely it overtook him. He began to fear that this was how his life would remain: tense, joyless, organized around avoiding reminders and dreading the next reaction. At the same time, some part of him still hopes that if he can finally face what happened without going numb or collapsing into guilt, life might recover some meaning, and he might feel like himself again.
